ceb.title: Maria - Ina sa Dios
ceb.question: Giunsa nato ma-apod ang Ina sa Dios si Maria?
ceb.answer: Ang tawag sa Ina sa Dios (Theotokos) si Maria dili tungod kay siya gimugna sa Dios, apan tungod kay siya nanganak sa Iyang Anak nga si Hesus, kinsa mao'y tinuod nga Dios ug tinuod nga tawo. Sa Konseho sa Ephesus (431 AD), gideklarar sa simbahan nga ang Maria mao'y Theotokos o Ina sa Dios, aron protektahan ang pagtuo sa kabubut-on sa Kristo. Kung si Jesus mao'y Dios, ug si Maria mao'y Iyang ina, busa si Maria mao'y Ina sa Dios.

en.title: Mary, Mother of God (Theotokos)
en.question: How can Mary be the Mother of God? God has no beginning, so isn't this blasphemy?
en.answer: Calling Mary the Mother of God (Theotokos, 'God-bearer') is a statement about Christ, not a claim that Mary predates the divinity. Because Jesus is one divine Person with two natures, human and divine, the one whom Mary conceived and bore is truly God the Son. Motherhood refers to a person, not merely a nature; a mother bears her child, not just his human body, so Mary is mother of the Person who is God. Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, already confessed this when she called Mary 'the mother of my Lord' (Lk 1:43). The title was solemnly defined at the Council of Ephesus in 431 to defend the truth that Jesus is a single, undivided divine Person. To deny Mary this title is to divide Christ into two persons, the heresy of Nestorius; thus Theotokos safeguards the deity of Christ himself.
en.answer_full:
> "Behold, from now on will all ages call me blessed. The Mighty One has done great things for me, and holy is his name."
> — Luke 1:48–49 (NABRE)

The title *Mother of God* (*Theotokos* in Greek, *Dei Genetrix* in Latin) is not a Marian privilege invented to exalt Mary — it is a christological definition required by the doctrine of the Incarnation. Its logic is simple: (1) Mary is the mother of Jesus. (2) Jesus is God. (3) Therefore Mary is the Mother of God. The controversy at Ephesus (431 AD) was not ultimately about Mary but about Christ: whether the Person born of Mary was truly the eternal Son of God, or merely a human person who came to be associated with the divine Word.

---

## The Biblical Foundation

### Luke 1:35 — What Is Born Is the Son of God

*"The holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God."* (Luke 1:35, NABRE)

The angel does not say that the Son of God will *inhabit* the child Mary bears — he says the child *will be called holy, the Son of God*. The One born of Mary is identified as the Son of God himself. The verb is *gennaō* (to be born, to be begotten) — the same word used of the Son's eternal generation from the Father (John 1:14, Hebrews 1:5). Mary does not bear a human person later assumed by the Son — she bears the Son.

### Luke 1:41–43 — Elizabeth's Testimony

*"And how does this happen to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?"* (Luke 1:43, NABRE)

Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, addresses Mary as *mētēr tou Kyriou mou* — *Mother of my Lord*. In the Septuagint, *Kyrios* (Lord) translates *YHWH* — the divine name. Elizabeth's Spirit-inspired recognition is that the one in Mary's womb is the Lord God himself. Luke 1:43 is the scriptural equivalent of *Theotokos*.

### Galatians 4:4 — God Sent His Son, Born of a Woman

*"But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to ransom those under the law."* (Galatians 4:4, NABRE)

Paul identifies the subject of the Incarnation as God's *Son* — not a human person later elevated. The Son of God was *born of a woman* — not simply associated with one. This is the Pauline Theotokos: the eternal divine Son took birth from a human mother.

### John 1:14 — The Word Became Flesh

*"And the Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us."* (John 1:14, NABRE)

The Word (identified as God in John 1:1) *became* flesh — did not inhabit flesh. This becoming is the Incarnation, and it occurred in Mary's womb. The Incarnate Word is the Son born of Mary.

---

## The Christological Stakes: The Nestorian Controversy

### Nestorius's Error

Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople (installed 428 AD), objected to *Theotokos* and proposed *Christotokos* (Mother of Christ) on the grounds that Mary bore a human nature, not the divine nature. His position implied — however he personally intended it — that there are two persons in Christ: a human person born of Mary, and the divine Word. He reportedly preached: *"Mary did not bear the Godhead — the Godhead did not die on the cross."*

### St. Cyril's Response: Communicatio Idiomatum

St. Cyril of Alexandria identified the error: Nestorius was dividing the one Christ into two subjects. Catholic theology insists on the **communicatio idiomatum** — the *communication of attributes*: because Christ is one Person, what is true of that Person according to either nature can be attributed to him simpliciter.

Therefore:
- *"The Son of God was born of Mary"* ✓
- *"Mary is the Mother of the Son of God"* ✓
- *"Mary is the Mother of God"* ✓

And on the passion:
- *"God died on the cross"* ✓ (in his human nature, but *he* — the divine Person — died)

None of this attributes the eternal generation of the divine nature to Mary. It attributes to the *Person* of the Son what happened to him in his human nature — including his birth from Mary.

---

## The Key Theological Distinction: Person vs. Nature

| Claim | Correct? | Explanation |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| Mary is the Mother of the divine *nature* | No | The divine nature is eternal; it has no mother |
| Mary is the Mother of the divine *Person* (who has a human nature) | Yes | Motherhood is personal, not natural |
| Mary bore a human person later united to the Word | No | Nestorian error — there is one Person in Christ, not two |
| Mary bore the divine Person of the Son in his human nature | Yes | Orthodox doctrine of the Incarnation |

Motherhood is a *personal* relationship. A mother does not give birth to a *nature* — she gives birth to a *person*. The Person born of Mary is the eternal Son of God. Therefore Mary is the Mother of God.

---

## Church Fathers

> "If anyone does not acknowledge that Emmanuel is truly God and that the Holy Virgin is, therefore, Theotokos, inasmuch as she bore in the flesh the Word of God made flesh — let him be anathema."
> — St. Cyril of Alexandria, *Third Letter to Nestorius* (c. AD 430)

> "The Lord has come forth from the womb of the virgin as a man, and Mary is called Theotokos not because she gave birth to the divinity, but because she gave birth to the human nature that was deified."
> — St. John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, III.12 (c. AD 743)

> "He who was begotten of the Father before the ages was born in the last age of the Virgin Mother."
> — St. Leo the Great, *Sermon 21* (c. AD 440)

---

## Ecumenical Council: Ephesus (431 AD)

The Third Ecumenical Council (Ephesus, 431 AD) condemned Nestorius and defined:

> *"If anyone does not confess that God is truly Emmanuel, and that on this account the Holy Virgin is the Mother of God (Theotokos) — for according to the flesh she gave birth to the Word of God become flesh — let him be anathema."*
> — Council of Ephesus, Anathema 1 (AD 431)

The popular reception of this definition was extraordinary — crowds in Ephesus lit torches and carried the bishops through the streets in celebration.

---

## CCC References

| Reference | Teaching |
|-----------|----------|
| CCC 495 | Mary is the Mother of God — she truly became the Mother of God by conceiving the eternal Son |
| CCC 466 | The title Theotokos was first defended and then defined at Ephesus |
| CCC 509 | Mary is truly the Mother of God because she is the Mother of the eternal Son made man |
| CCC 722 | The Holy Spirit prepared Mary so that she would become the worthy Mother of God |

---

## Common Objections

**"Mary is only the mother of Jesus's human nature, not of God."**

Motherhood is a relationship with a *person*, not with a *nature*. When your mother gave birth to you, she gave birth to *you* — a whole person — not merely to your body. Similarly, Mary gave birth to the Son of God — a whole Person who is both divine and human. The one Person born of Mary is the eternal Son of God. To deny this is Nestorianism — the heresy that divides Christ into two persons.

**"Calling Mary 'Mother of God' elevates her above God."**

The title says nothing about Mary's nature or status relative to God. It describes the relationship between Mary and her Son. A mother is not exalted *above* her son merely by being his mother — she is exalted by being intimately related to him. Calling Mary the Mother of God exalts Christ — it insists that the Person born of her is truly God, not merely a holy man or an exalted creature.

**"This title isn't in the Bible."**

Elizabeth's Spirit-inspired greeting in Luke 1:43 — *"the mother of my Lord"* — is the scriptural equivalent, using *Kyrios* (Lord/YHWH). The *word* Theotokos is not in the Bible; neither is the word Trinity. Both are precise theological formulations that express what Scripture teaches. Luke 1:43, Galatians 4:4, and John 1:14 together entail that the Person born of Mary is the eternal divine Son.

---

The title *Mother of God* is ultimately about Jesus, not Mary. It insists that the Christ born of Mary is not a deified human person or a human vehicle for a divine presence, but the eternal Son of God himself, who took human flesh from his Mother. To confess Mary as Theotokos is to confess the full reality of the Incarnation — God truly became man, truly took flesh from a human woman, was truly born, grew, suffered, and died — and in doing so, the relationship between this woman and her Son is the most extraordinary in human history.

tl.title: Maria bilang Ina ng Dios
tl.question: Bakit tinatawag ng mga Katoliko si Maria na 'Ina ng Dios'?
tl.answer: Tinatawag ng mga Katoliko si Maria na 'Ina ng Dios' (Theotokos sa Griyego) hindi dahil siya ay umiiral bago si Dios, kundi dahil siya ay nanganak kay Jesus Cristo, na buong Dios at buong tao. Kung si Jesus ay Dios, si Maria ay tunay na ina na nanganak kay Dios. Ang titulong ito ay ipinagtanggol sa Council of Ephesus noong 431 AD at nagpapatibay sa katotohanan ng Incarnation - na ang Dios ay tunay na nagkatawang tao sa sinapupunan ni Maria.
